findings.printedLatin: Quid facimus nos? Ergo non meditabimur in mandatis ejus, neque investigabimur semitas illius, et requiescere poterit cor nostrum donec inveniat illam. Tantum ipsis sermonibus persequamur illam
findings.englishAsRendered: What do we do? Therefore we shall not meditate on his commandments, nor shall we search out her paths, and our heart will be able to rest until it find her. Only let us pursue her with these very words
findings.conjecture: The run is a chain of rhetorical questions ('Shall we then not meditate on his commandments, nor search out her paths? and will our heart be able to rest until it find her?'), or else the source has dropped a negative before requiescere (nec requiescere poterit cor nostrum donec inveniat illam). Either way the English must carry the negative force: we ARE to meditate and search, and the heart can NOT rest until it finds wisdom.
findings.whyContradiction: The very next sentence commands the opposite of the flat assertion our page makes: 'Tantum ipsis sermonibus persequamur illam: et si forte inventio differatur, pascat interim nos inquisitio illius super omnia' — 'Only let us pursue her with these very words; and if perhaps the finding be deferred, let the search for her meanwhile feed us above all things.' A writer who has just said 'we shall not meditate, nor shall we search out her paths' cannot immediately exhort to unresting pursuit; and 'our heart will be able to rest until it find her' reverses the donec-clause, which exists to deny rest before the finding.

findings.printedLatin: sed nec admonitus quidem velle possit aut non esse quod male est, aut esse quod male non est. Nam quod est, male est, et quod esse deberet, male non est. Et quod vult aut non esse, quod est, aut esse quod non est: hoc utroque pejus est.
findings.englishAsRendered: but cannot even when admonished will either that what evilly is should not be, or that what evilly is not should be. ... And that it wills either that what is should not be, or that what is not should be: this is worse than both.
findings.conjecture: Et quod NON vult aut non esse quod est, aut esse quod non est: hoc utroque pejus est — 'And that it does NOT will either that what is should cease to be, or that what is not should be: this is worse than both.'
findings.whyContradiction: The clause two sentences earlier states flatly that the mind 'nec admonitus quidem velle possit' these very two things — it cannot even when admonished WILL them. Printed as it stands, the mind now does will them, and the summing 'hoc utroque pejus est' ('this is worse than both') then calls a good willing worse than the two evils just enumerated (that what is, is evil; that what ought to be, is not). Only the negative makes the third item a third, worse evil.

findings.printedLatin: Magnum quoddam exspectavimus, et illud propositum grande omnes non attentos et exspectantes jam fecerat.
findings.englishAsRendered: We expected something great, and that grand purpose had already made all men not attentive and expectant.
findings.conjecture: omnes NOS attentos et exspectantes jam fecerat — 'had already made us all attentive and expectant' (nos misread as non).
findings.whyContradiction: The immediately preceding clause is 'Magnum quoddam exspectavimus' — 'We expected something great' — and the printed sentence's own second adjective is *exspectantes*, 'expectant'. 'Not attentive AND expectant' contradicts itself inside the phrase, and the following line ('Quis enim de tanta promissione exiguum aliquid exire posse putaret?' — who would think anything scanty could come of so great a promise?) depends on the audience being keyed up, not inattentive.

findings.printedLatin: et veritatem quam intus caecata a fonte haurire non potest, quasi per rivulos quosdam visibilium arescentibus praecordiis saltem fugere conatur
findings.englishAsRendered: and the truth which, blinded within, it cannot draw from the fountain, it attempts at least to flee, with parched inward parts, as it were through certain rivulets of visible things
findings.conjecture: saltem SUGERE conatur — 'it attempts at least to SUCK (draw) through certain rivulets of visible things' (f/s confusion; the long-s reading).
findings.whyContradiction: The same sentence says the mind cannot *haurire* (draw/drink) the truth *a fonte*, and describes it as *arescentibus praecordiis*, with parched inward parts, resorting to *rivulos* — a sustained drinking image in which the mind is chasing truth outward, not fleeing it. The whole surrounding argument (it 'seeks hungrily, as it were the food of understanding, in the knowledge of those things which are without') is of a mind pursuing truth through visible things; 'flee' reverses the direction of the motion the metaphor requires.
